title: DAVE: Distribution-aware Attribution via ViT Gradient Decomposition
claim: Our attribution method yields sharp, pixel-level maps that trace each object's class-specific fine structure.
layout: 1 row of 3 image pairs, left-to-right, input beside attribution heatmap
description: A single horizontal strip of six square images arranged as three input/attribution pairs. Each natural ImageNet photo (a monarch butterfly on purple flowers, two violins on white cloth, and an arched steel bridge against blue sky) is followed by its attribution map. The maps are drawn on a black background with a purple-to-orange-to-yellow colormap. They trace fine structure: butterfly wing veins and spots, violin outlines and strings, and bridge girders and cables. There are no arrows, labels, text or math. The eye goes first to the bright, saturated heatmaps beside the photos. The overall message is that the attributions are crisp and detailed.
caption: DAVE provides fine-grained, pixel-level attributions that capture class-specific structural patterns present in each object. ImageNet-1k (Russakovsky et al., 2015) samples and corresponding DAVE attributions for DeiT III-B-16/224 (Touvron et al., 2022).
abstract: Vision Transformers (ViTs) have become a dominant architecture in computer vision, yet producing stable and high-resolution attribution maps for these models remains challenging. Architectural components such as patch embeddings and attention routing often introduce structured artifacts in pixel-level explanations, causing many existing methods to rely on coarse patch-level attributions. We introduce DAVE \textit{(\underline{D}istribution-aware \underline{A}ttribution via \underline{V}iT Gradient D\underline{E}composition)}, a mathematically grounded attribution method for ViTs based on a structured decomposition of the input gradient. By exploiting architectural properties of ViTs, DAVE isolates locally equivariant and stable components of the effective input--output mapping. It separates these from architecture-induced artifacts and other sources of instability.
